claims.text: Mechanical-property differences between the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its single-phase FCC quaternary and ternary subsets are primarily governed by chemical short-range order.
Reducing the number of alloy constituents promotes enhanced chemical short-range order.
Chemical short-range order modifies local lattice distortions.
Chemical short-range order modifies stacking-fault energies.
Changes in local lattice distortion and stacking-fault energy alter dislocation behavior.
Altered dislocation behavior controls differences in yield strength and ductility.
Identical thermomechanical processing will ensure comparable grain structures and phase stability across the tested alloys.
Enhanced short-range order develops more readily in alloys with fewer constituents.
Enhanced short-range order creates local variations in lattice distortion.
Enhanced short-range order alters energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Quaternary and ternary alloys with enhanced short-range order will exhibit statistically significant mechanical-property differences from the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Yield strength and ductility will correlate with short-range-order intensity.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline has a more uniform elemental distribution than the proposed quaternary and ternary variants.
There is limited evidence of pronounced chemical short-range order in the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline.
Chemical short-range order can be quantitatively characterized using atom-probe tomography or X-ray diffuse scattering.
Stacking-fault energy can be inferred using TEM or diffraction methods.
